transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-18
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Samir V. (joined late), Chris Wu (Atlas CTO), Maya Patel (Atlas SRE), Leo Ramos (Atlas ML Engineer), Anika Flores (Atlas Product)

Summary: Redwood led a technical deep dive focused on observability and tracing for token-level metrics. Atlas wants to ensure they can see per-token latencies, KV cache hit rates, batching queue times, and surface those in their Grafana via OpenTelemetry/OTLP to validate cost/latency trade-offs and support an eventual private/VPC deployment.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call - Jordan Blake from Redwood AE, Priya Shah our SE.
[00:08] Chris: Hey Chris here, Atlas - CTO. Maya, Leo, Anika on our side.
[00:13] Priya: Great, objective for today is to walk through how we instrument for token-level traces, what metrics we expose around KV cache and batching, and how that maps into dashboards. We'll also touch on OTLP in VPC.
[00:25] Maya: sounds good, we specifically want to capture cache hit rate and per-token latency so we can compare hosted vs dedicated economics.
[00:30] Jordan: Awesome. Priya, do you want to start on the tracing model?
[00:33] Priya: Sure. So at a high level we emit spans for request lifecycle then for token generation we create nested spans per token or per chunk depending on config. The common approach is to emit a short-lived span at token boundaries with attributes: model, model_version, shard_id, sequence_length, token_index, is_cache_hit (boolean), batch_size.
[00:55] Leo: sorry can I interrupt, token-level spans sound heavy — what's the perf overhead?
[00:59] Priya: good question. There's measurable overhead; in our internal benchmarks full token spans add about 5-12% tail latency depending on exporter and sampling. We usually recommend static sampling for high-volume endpoints or sampling only error/slow requests, and emitting aggregated per-token metrics (counts/histograms) in addition to traces.
[01:20] Chris: ok, so we do a mix — keep traces sampled, but expose detailed counters for hit rates and per-token histograms?
[01:26] Priya: Exactly. So OTLP pipeline: SDK -> local agent (optional) -> OTLP collector in your VPC -> Grafana/Tempo/Prometheus. Agent helps batch and compress telemetry, which is useful in private deployments.
[01:40] Maya: can you show what the metric names and labels look like?
[01:44] Priya: Sure, example metrics we surface: redwood.request.latency_seconds (per request), redwood.token.latency_seconds (histogram per token), redwood.kv.cache_hit_total and redwood.kv.cache_miss_total (counters), redwood.batch.queue_time_seconds, redwood.model.quantized_inference_seconds. Labels: tenant_id, route, model, model_version, shard, env (prod/staging), seq_len_bucket.
[02:08] Anika: seq_len_bucket — how do you pick buckets?
[02:12] Priya: We typically align buckets to common request sizes: [<=32, 33-128, 129-512, >512]. That lets you drill into p50/p90/p99 by sequence length.
[02:22] [02:22] Jordan: note — transcription glitch there, Priya said p50/p90, just flagging for notes.
[02:27] Chris: For KV cache, how do you link a token-level cache hit to the trace?
[02:31] Priya: We attach a boolean attribute is_cache_hit and also emit an event on the span when a KV cache lookup occurs. If hit, we include cache_key and hit_ttl_ms sometimes. In metrics we also increment per-tenant cache_hit_total with labels including seq_len_bucket and model so dashboards can calculate hit rate.
[02:48] Leo: does the cache key contain PII or customer data? That's a compliance concern for us.
[02:53] Priya: We strip or hash keys by default and recommend not sending raw prompt content in attributes. We support hashing with customer-provided salt in private deployments.
[03:05] Maya: ok good. Next, batching visibility — we need queue time, batch size distribution, and per-batch tail latency.
[03:13] Priya: We emit redwood.batch.queue_time_seconds as histogram with labels batch_size, route, model. Also span events on batch creation and dispatch with timestamps so span-based traces show the queue wait. This is useful to separate queueing vs inference time.
[03:29] Chris: For our SLA docs we need token-p90 latency and cost per 1k tokens. Can you help map metrics to cost?
[03:36] Jordan: we have a cost breakdown exporter that emits redwood.cost.tokens_consumed_total by tenant_id and model_version. Combining that with token latency histograms you can build panels for cost vs p90 latency. Priya will share example dashboard.
[03:51] [03:51] Priya: quick note on quantization — we emit redwood.model.quantized_inference_seconds plus model_variant label (e.g., float16, int8-ggml). This lets you compare latency delta when using quantized runtimes. There's also an accuracy/regression signal we link to eval runs.
[04:10] Leo: about private/VPC — can we host the OTLP collector inside our VPC and not send telemetry outside?
[04:16] Priya: yes, for Redwood Private you can route telemetry to your collector. We can support OTLP over gRPC to your collector endpoint, or push to a sidecar. For security we support MTLS and we can also accept encrypted payloads to our control plane if needed, but most customers route to their own backends.
[04:34] Maya: ok, what about SSO/role-based access for who can view traces?
[04:38] Jordan: Redwood Console integrates with SAML/SSO and we propagate tenant_id in telemetry labels. For private deployments, you control dashboard access in your Grafana/observability stack; Redwood can provide a read-only dashboard JSON.
[04:51] Anika: can you demo a sample dashboard real quick?
[04:54] Priya: I'll share a static export — (screen share noted) Key panels: token p50/p90/p99, cache hit rate over time, batch queue time heatmap, model_variant comparison, cost per 1k tokens. We'll attach the JSON to the follow-up.
[05:12] [05:12] Chris: switching gear — how does tracing propagate when requests go through our front-end service into Redwood in VPC? Do we maintain trace-id?
[05:20] Priya: We accept parent trace context via W3C tracecontext or OTLP. If your frontend sends traceparent header, Redwood will use it as parent span so the full end-to-end trace is preserved. We also support baggage for tenant-scoped metadata.
[05:34] Leo: sampling policy? We want consistent sampling across services.
[05:38] Priya: You can set sampling at your OTLP collector or at Redwood SDK. Common pattern: centralized sampler at collector for consistent sampling decisions. We can provide guidance on sampling rates (e.g., 0.1% full token spans, 100% aggregated metrics).
[05:53] Maya: what's the size and cost impact of emitting token-level spans to Tempo or Jaeger?
[05:58] Priya: Token-level spans can blow up event volume — assume 10-30x increase vs request-only traces depending on sequence lengths. That's why we recommend either sampled traces + aggregated metrics and histograms, or using a local agent to batch/compress. For customers using Tempo, we point them at bucket retention and indexing strategies.
[06:18] Chris: do you have a reference Grafana dashboard link or repo?
[06:22] Priya: yes, we'll send dashboard JSON and a small repo with OTEL collector config and sample Prometheus rules.
[06:28] Jordan: quick check — any regulatory or SOC2 concerns for telemetry?
[06:31] Maya: we need to confirm we can avoid sending raw PII and that logs containing prompts are never exported.
[06:38] Priya: Agreed — by default we don't put prompt text in attributes; logs that include prompts are disabled for export and we recommend hashing keys. We'll attach our security docs which cover telemetry practices.
[06:51] Chris: about KV cache — how do you handle cache consistency for on-prem deployments?
[06:56] Priya: For Private we support local KV caches per shard with optional cross-shard replication. For observability we emit replication lag metrics and per-shard cache_hit_total so you can see divergence.
[07:09] Anika: can we alert on cache hit rate drop?
[07:12] Priya: Yes. Example alert: cache_hit_rate < 0.6 sustained for 5m for a route at p95. We'll include Prometheus rules.
[07:21] Leo: when you instrument batch queueing, is it easy to attribute delay to a specific tenant when mixed-tenancy is used?
[07:27] Priya: We label batch metrics with tenant_id and route; if batches are multi-tenant, we record per-tenant contributions (we sample or tag requests entering batch). There's some heuristics but it's possible to approximate per-tenant queuing impact. For full isolation, dedicated pools are recommended.
[07:43] Chris: tradeoffs — we want lower cost than hosted but decent latency. How do we use observability to choose dedicated vs hosted?
[07:50] Jordan: Observability helps by showing per-token cost, tail p99; if your workload is high QPS with predictable seq lengths, dedicated (or reserved) is cost-effective. If you have spiky traffic and strict isolation, Private with VPC might be better. We'll help analyze once we get your traffic profile.
[08:05] Maya: one last technical bit — quantization labels, how do you track model quality regressions with quantized variants?
[08:12] Priya: We tie quantized_variant label to evaluation runs and to a quality monitoring system that tracks prompt set failure rates. If quality drift exceeds threshold after a rollout we trigger an alert and automatic rollback.
[08:24] [08:24] Samir (joined): sorry I'm late, jumped in — any open questions?
[08:28] Chris: we want to see a concrete example of end-to-end OTLP config + Grafana.
[08:32] Samir: we'll make sure sample configs include MTLS config for collector and an OTLP pipeline for Prometheus and Tempo.
[08:39] Jordan: ok, timeline wise - sending docs this week, run bench in early March. anything else?
[08:46] Maya: also need a list of what telemetry touches the control plane vs stays in our VPC.
[08:50] Priya: noted — we'll include a matrix in the security doc.
[08:55] Anika: thanks — can you include sample dashboards showing cost per 1k tokens?
[08:59] Priya: yes.
[09:03] Jordan: recap of next steps (see action items). Thanks everyone.
[09:08] Chris: thanks, good session.
[09:11] Meeting end.
